name: Reinke Oedema
aliases: Polypoid degeneration of the vocal folds
polypoid degeneration of the vocal folds

clinicalPearls: The accumulation of gelatinous fluid within Reinke's space (the superficial layer of the lamina propria) of the vocal folds, producing diffuse polypoid swelling that is usually bilateral.
The hallmark symptom is a progressively low-pitched, gruff, hoarse voice, and it is a classic cause of an abnormally deep, masculine-sounding voice in women.
Cigarette smoking is the dominant risk factor, with vocal overuse, laryngopharyngeal reflux and hypothyroidism as important contributors.
Diagnosis is by laryngoscopy and videostroboscopy showing floppy, fluid-filled polypoid folds with an increased mucosal wave.
Because almost all patients are smokers, coexisting laryngeal dysplasia or carcinoma must be excluded, and any leukoplakia, ulceration or asymmetry warrants biopsy.
First-line management targets the causes: smoking cessation, voice therapy, and treatment of reflux and hypothyroidism.
Persistent, severe or airway-compromising disease is treated with microlaryngeal surgery, incising the superior fold and evacuating the gelatinous material while preserving mucosa.
Overaggressive resection or operating on both folds at the same sitting risks scarring, anterior web formation and permanent dysphonia.
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic irritation of the vocal fold epithelium, predominantly from tobacco smoke and compounded by phonotrauma, laryngopharyngeal reflux and hypothyroidism, increases vascular permeability and impairs drainage within Reinke's space. This potential space is normally loose, sparsely vascular and devoid of lymphatics, so fluid and gelatinous mucoid material accumulate readily within the superficial lamina propria and expand the fold into a floppy, polypoid structure. The added mass lowers the fundamental frequency of vocal fold vibration, producing the characteristic deep, hoarse voice, and when severe the redundant tissue can prolapse and obstruct the glottic airway. Changes are typically bilateral and, in early stages, largely reversible once the irritant, particularly smoking, is removed.
additionalDifferentials: Laryngeal dysplasia or carcinoma (must be excluded in smokers)
additionalInvestigations: Flexible or rigid laryngoscopy with videostroboscopy
Microlaryngoscopy and biopsy of any suspicious mucosal lesion to exclude malignancy
Perceptual and acoustic voice assessment by speech and language therapy
Documentation of smoking history and cessation support
Airway assessment where bulky disease causes obstruction
redFlags: Stridor or airway obstruction from bulky polypoid folds
A unilateral lesion, ulceration, leukoplakia or fold fixation suggesting malignancy
Referred otalgia, dysphagia or a neck mass
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is good; with smoking cessation and voice care early disease can regress, and surgery reliably improves the voice. The deep vocal quality may only partly normalise, and continued smoking causes recurrence.
pitfalls: Assuming disease is benign and failing to exclude carcinoma in a smoker.
Operating on both folds simultaneously and risking an anterior glottic web and scarring.
Neglecting smoking cessation, leading to recurrence after surgery.
Overlooking untreated hypothyroidism or reflux as perpetuating factors.
Setting unrealistic expectations that the voice will return to a high pitch.
management: Complete smoking cessation is the cornerstone, since removal of tobacco irritation allows early polypoid change to regress and prevents recurrence
Voice therapy with a speech and language therapist to reduce phonotrauma and correct vocal overuse
Treat contributing laryngopharyngeal reflux with proton-pump inhibitor therapy and antireflux lifestyle measures
Correct coexisting hypothyroidism with thyroid hormone replacement
Microlaryngoscopic phonosurgery with a lateral cordotomy and evacuation of the gelatinous material, preserving the mucosal edge, for persistent dysphonia or airway compromise
Emergency airway assessment and intervention when severe bilateral polypoid folds prolapse and threaten the glottic airway
Surveillance laryngoscopy with biopsy of any leukoplakia, ulceration or asymmetry to exclude coexisting laryngeal dysplasia or carcinoma
Refer to laryngology with joint speech and language therapy input for combined voice and structural rehabilitation
